questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: convert a decimal to binary by hand and explain the reversal
questions.stem: Trace this converter and state the string displayed. n <- 41. bits <- "". WHILE n > 0: bits <- bits + STRING(n MOD 2). n <- n DIV 2. DISPLAY REVERSE(bits).

options.text: 101001 is displayed; each bit arrives least significant first, so the string is reversed
options.misconception: believes the appended bits are already in most significant order

options.text: 100101 is displayed; the bits are appended as found and never reversed afterwards
options.misconception: believes the loop produces digits in their final reading order

options.text: 110101 is displayed; the loop divides before testing, so the leading bit is doubled
options.misconception: believes the division happens before the remainder is recorded

options.text: 1000101 is displayed; the loop takes one extra pass and appends a final zero bit
options.misconception: believes the loop continues until the quotient is below zero

questions.explanation: Repeated division by two hands back the remainders from the least significant bit upward, so the loop builds 100101 and the reversal turns that into 101001, which is 32 + 8 + 1 = 41. The tempting answer is B, which is the string before the reversal and is the mistake almost everyone makes once; the digits are all correct there, so it looks plausible, but it reads as 37. Reading the pseudocode is enough to settle it, because the remainder is always the low bit of the current quotient.
questions.hint: Write each remainder as it is produced, then read that list backwards.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Signed overflow in a fixed width
questions.learningObjective: work out the stored value of a signed overflow
questions.stem: A signed field of 4 bits (values -8 to 7) holds each result. Trace this snippet and state the value displayed. a <- 6. b <- 5. sum <- a + b. stored <- sum. IF stored > 7: stored <- stored - 16. DISPLAY stored.

options.text: -5 is displayed; an overflow past 7 re-enters the field at the negative end
options.misconception: believes a signed overflow keeps the arithmetic result unchanged

options.text: 11 is displayed; the field holds whatever value the addition produced
options.misconception: believes a four-bit field stores any result handed to it

options.text: 27 is displayed; the bit that fell off the top is folded back into the low bits
options.misconception: believes the discarded high bit is added back rather than dropped

options.text: 0 is displayed; a signed overflow is defined to leave the field cleared
options.misconception: believes an overflow resets the field to zero by definition

questions.explanation: The addition gives 11, which is past the largest value 7 that four signed bits can hold, so the field re-enters at the bottom: 11 - 16 = -5, and the bit pattern 1011 is read as minus 5. The tempting answer is B, which is the arithmetic result rather than the stored one, and it fails because the field has only four bits to give. The tempting answer is C, which keeps the bit that overflowed, and a field that kept it would not be four bits wide.
questions.hint: Work out the bit pattern of 11, then read those four bits as a signed value.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: negate a value by hand inside a fixed-width field
questions.stem: A sensor stores readings in an 8-bit unsigned field. Trace this snippet and state the value displayed. x <- 5. y <- 0. y <- (0 - x) MOD 256. DISPLAY y.

options.text: 251 is displayed; negating inside 8 bits means 256 minus the value, not minus 5
options.misconception: believes a small negative result survives a modulo 256 unchanged

options.text: 5 is displayed; taking a modulo of a small value returns that same value
options.misconception: believes the modulus leaves a value under 256 completely untouched

options.text: 250 is displayed; the value is subtracted from 255 instead of from 256
options.misconception: confuses the modulus with the largest value a field can hold

options.text: 0 is displayed; a subtraction that goes below zero is defined to clamp at zero
options.misconception: believes modular subtraction clamps to zero instead of wrapping around

questions.explanation: The modulus turns the negative result -5 into a non-negative code by adding the field size once, giving 256 - 5 = 251, and the bit pattern 11111011 is the usual two's complement stand-in for minus 5. The tempting answer is B, which applies the modulus as though small values passed through untouched, and it ignores that -5 itself is below zero. The tempting answer is C, which subtracts from 255 because that is the largest storable value, but the wrap needs the field size, not the largest value in it.
questions.hint: Work out the value, then add the field size until the result is not negative.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: convert a raw sensor code into a physical value
questions.stem: A 12-bit sensor spans 0 to 5 V, so its 4096 codes cover 0 to 4095 (values -1 never occur). Trace this snippet and state the value displayed. raw <- 3072. value <- raw * 5 / 4096. DISPLAY value.

options.text: 3.75 is displayed; the code count is divided by the 4096 codes that span the range
options.misconception: believes the raw code is already a measurement in volts

options.text: 15 is displayed; the code count is multiplied by the full-scale value to scale it
options.misconception: believes scaling means multiplying by the top of the range

options.text: 3072 is displayed; the raw code is shown with no scale factor applied at all
options.misconception: believes a scaled reading is reported as the code the hardware produced

options.text: 0.75 is displayed; the scale factor is applied before the count is divided
options.misconception: believes dividing first and scaling after gives the same answer

questions.explanation: A code is a fraction of the range, not a measurement, so the count is multiplied by the 5 V span and divided by the 4096 codes, giving 15360 / 4096 = 3.75. The tempting answer is B, which multiplies by the span without dividing by the code count, and the result is five times too large because a code stands for a five-thousandths slice of the range, not for the whole thing. Dividing first, as D does, is the tempting shortcut that also fails, since 3072 / 4096 is 0.75 and 0.75 * 5 is 3.75 only if the order is reversed properly.
questions.hint: Work out what fraction of the range 3072 is, then multiply by 5.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Counting the codes a run coder emits
questions.learningObjective: count the run codes a coder produces for a stated bit string
questions.stem: A run-length coder stores the bit string 00011000 as run codes (one code per run). Trace this snippet and state the value displayed. s <- "00011000". out <- 0. i <- 1. WHILE i <= 8: j <- i. WHILE j <= 8 AND s[j] = s[i]: j <- j + 1. out <- out + 1. i <- j. DISPLAY out.

options.text: 3 is displayed; the encoder emits one code per run, and this string has three runs
options.misconception: believes run-length coding emits one code for every bit it stores

options.text: 8 is displayed; one code is produced for each bit regardless of the repeats
options.misconception: believes a run coder never saves anything over the raw bits

options.text: 2 is displayed; only the two distinct bit values are counted, not the separate runs
options.misconception: believes a run coder stores one code per distinct value present

options.text: 4 is displayed; the final run is dropped because the loop stops one index early
options.misconception: believes the outer loop condition discards the last run it finds

questions.explanation: The string splits into three runs, namely 000, then 11, then 000, and the encoder writes one code per run, so the count is 3 rather than the 8 bits it started with. The tempting answer is B, which is what the coder would emit if repeats carried no benefit, and it is worth checking precisely because a short run count is where the saving comes from. The tempting answer is D, which suspects the guard, but the inner loop advances j past the last index so the final run is still counted and i simply leaves the range.
questions.hint: List the runs in the string before reading the counters.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: convert a decimal fraction to binary by doubling
questions.stem: A converter keeps 4 bits after the point (the weights 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625). Trace this snippet and state the string displayed. f <- 0.625. bits <- "". REPEAT 4 TIMES: f <- f * 2. IF f >= 1: bits <- bits + "1". f <- f - 1. ELSE: bits <- bits + "0". DISPLAY bits.

options.text: 1010 is displayed; each doubling contributes 0.5, then 0.25, then 0.125, then 0.0625
options.misconception: believes the bits are produced by halving the fraction each pass

options.text: 1000 is displayed; the loop stops at the first whole digit and pads the rest with zeros
options.misconception: believes a fraction with an early whole digit has no later bits

options.text: 1100 is displayed; a remainder above a half is rounded up instead of carried down
options.misconception: believes each pass rounds rather than keeping the exact remainder

options.text: 0110 is displayed; the first doubling is recorded as a leading zero instead of a one
options.misconception: believes the whole-number part of a fraction is discarded as unused padding

questions.explanation: Doubling the fraction moves the next binary digit into view each pass: 0.625 doubles to 1.25 so the first digit is 1 and 0.25 is carried, 0.25 doubles to 0.5 giving 0, 0.5 doubles to 1 giving 1 with nothing left, and the last pass gives 0, producing 1010 which is exactly 0.625. The tempting answer is B, which stops the arithmetic as soon as a whole digit appears, but the whole digit is only the first half of the number, and the carried remainder is what supplies the rest.
questions.hint: Double the fraction each pass, subtract 1 when it reaches 1, and keep going.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Extracting a bit field with a mask
questions.learningObjective: extract the low bits of a value with a mask
questions.stem: A byte 202 (binary 11001010) holds four status flags in its four low bits. Trace this snippet and state the value displayed. b <- 202. flags <- b AND 15. DISPLAY flags.

options.text: 10 is displayed; the mask keeps the four low bits, which are 1010 in binary
options.misconception: believes a mask keeps the high bits because they carry more weight

options.text: 202 is displayed; a mask of all low bits set leaves the value unchanged
options.misconception: believes AND with 15 is an identity operation on any byte

options.text: 12 is displayed; the byte is read as the single hex digit C that it contains
options.misconception: believes one hex digit is the same thing as the low four bits

options.text: 15 is displayed; masking always produces the largest value the mask can express
options.misconception: believes a mask copies its own pattern into the result

questions.explanation: 202 is 11001010 in binary and the mask 15 is 00001111, so AND keeps the low four bits 1010 and returns 10, which is how packed flags are read back one field at a time. The tempting answer is B, which treats AND with 15 as harmless, and it is wrong because 15 is only all ones in the low four positions, so it clears everything above them. The tempting answer is C, which reads a byte as one hex digit; the byte CA has two hex digits and its low digit A happens to agree with 10, which is exactly the coincidence that makes this trap convincing.
questions.hint: Write 202 in binary, then write 15 in binary beneath it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Choosing a field width for a range
questions.learningObjective: size a field to hold a stated inclusive range
questions.stem: A turnstile counter must hold every whole number of visitors from 0 up to and including 1000. What is the smallest number of bits that can hold them all?
questions.explanation: The range 0 to 1000 inclusive is 1001 distinct values, and a field of n bits holds 2 to the power n of them, so 9 bits offer 512 and are too few while 10 bits offer 1024 and are enough. The off-by-one is the whole difficulty here, because a field sized for 1000 values would still be 10 bits, so counting from zero must be included rather than waved at. This is the sizing rule to keep for any stored count: decide the largest permitted value, then take the next power of two above it.
questions.hint: Count the values including zero, then compare with 512 and with 1024.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: work out the width a digit-per-field code needs
questions.stem: A fuel pump stores a reading such as 907 with each decimal digit kept on its own four bits. How many bits does that reading occupy?
questions.explanation: Keeping one digit per four bits spends 3 * 4 = 12 bits, and the cost is that only ten of each field's sixteen codes can ever occur, so six codes per digit are wasted. The same reading in plain binary needs only ten bits, since 907 is under 1024, which is the trade such a code makes: arithmetic on single digits becomes easy and space efficiency is surrendered. Any width calculation for a stored number has to start from the representation, because the representation is what sets the field size.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of digits by the bits each digit occupies.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: compare the value ranges of signed and unsigned fields
questions.stem: A 4-bit unsigned field offers 16 codes. The same width using two's complement offers 8 non-negative codes and 8 negative ones. What does that split show about the cost of a sign?

options.text: One code is spent on the sign, so the positive range is half the unsigned range
options.misconception: believes adding a sign leaves the number of usable codes unchanged

options.text: The negative codes are extra capacity, so the signed field holds 8 more values in total
options.misconception: believes negative values are stored in addition to the unsigned ones

options.text: Both fields can hold any 16 values, and only the reading of a bit changes
options.misconception: believes a signed field loses no codes compared with an unsigned one

options.text: The split is a naming convention, since either field can hold any 16 values
options.misconception: believes the range of a field is a matter of how it is labelled

questions.explanation: The top bit stops being a magnitude bit and becomes the sign, so four bits hold 0 to 7 rather than 0 to 15, and the price of a signed range is exactly half the positive range. The tempting answer is B, which counts negative values as a bonus, and it is wrong because a signed field has the same number of codes and spends one of them on the sign. The tempting answer is C, which is tempting only because the bit patterns are identical, and it confuses how a pattern is read with how many patterns exist.
questions.hint: Count the codes, then ask which one the sign takes for itself.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: convert a bit width into the bytes a record occupies
questions.stem: A status record gives each of eight sensors its own 4-bit field packed side by side. How many bytes does one such record occupy?
questions.explanation: Eight fields of 4 bits use 8 * 4 = 32 bits, and 32 bits is 4 bytes, so the packed record costs one byte per sensor pair instead of the eight bytes a byte-per-sensor layout would need. The rounding is exact here rather than approximate, which is the condition that makes packing worth doing at all, so a record width that does not divide into whole bytes is where padding starts to cost. The habit to keep is converting to bits first and to bytes last, in that order.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of fields by their width, then divide by eight.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a negative reading from an unsigned field
questions.stem: A sensor register holds 0 to 4095 and is documented as unsigned. A reading comes back as -1. What does that value tell you about what happened?

options.text: The raw count passed 4095 and wrapped, so the reading is really the top of the range
options.misconception: believes an unsigned register can hold a genuine negative reading

options.text: The sensor is measuring below its calibrated floor and reported it faithfully
options.misconception: believes a physical value below zero produces a negative register count

options.text: The register type is wrong, so a valid count of 4095 must be read as a large value
options.misconception: believes a documented unsigned field cannot be read as a negative number

options.text: The register was cleared, and an empty register always reads as negative one
options.misconception: believes a reset register holds minus one by definition

questions.explanation: An unsigned field has no negative values, so -1 is not a measurement at all but the code that appears when a count of 4096 is stored in 4096 codes, and that count is the very top of the range. The tempting answer is B, which treats the field as if it recorded a physical value rather than a position in a fixed list of codes. The tempting answer is also C, which is a fair question about the documentation and still not what the value itself says, because a read of -1 is a specific and recognisable wrap.
questions.hint: Ask which count would have to be stored to produce this pattern.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a counter that jumps from its maximum to zero
questions.stem: A well counter is stored in a 12-bit field and advances by one per visitor. It reads 4095, the next read is 0, and the day's grand total is short by one. What best explains all three facts?

options.text: The field wrapped after its 4096th count, so the counter restarted and lost its place
options.misconception: believes a field that has reached its maximum continues past it

options.text: A power cut cleared the field, and a cleared field always restarts from zero
options.misconception: believes every restart to zero is caused by a power cut

options.text: The counter stored a negative value, and a driver printed it as zero for display
options.misconception: believes a negative count is routinely displayed as zero

options.text: A rounding step in the driver skipped 4095, and rounding drops the largest value
options.misconception: believes a display rounding step can remove a specific reading

questions.explanation: A 12-bit field holds exactly 4096 codes, so the 4096th visitor pushes the stored value past the top and it comes back as 0, which loses that one count and explains the short total. The tempting answer is B, which reaches for a power cut because a reset also shows zero, but a reset is not needed to explain a value sitting exactly at the field's maximum one step earlier. The tempting answer is also D, which invents a display step; the counter is what read 4095 before the wrap.
questions.hint: Count how many distinct values a 12-bit field can hold.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish truncation from rounding when a field gets smaller
questions.stem: A reading of 4.6 must be stored in a field that holds whole numbers only. Which statement describes the difference between truncating that value and rounding it?

options.text: Truncation discards the fraction and keeps 4, while rounding moves it to the next whole number
options.misconception: believes truncating a fraction rounds it to the nearest value

options.text: Truncation and rounding both discard the fraction, and rounding also reports an error
options.misconception: believes rounding is truncation plus a warning about the value

options.text: Rounding discards the fraction, while truncation always moves up to the next number
options.misconception: believes truncation rounds a value up to the next whole number

options.text: Neither changes the value, since a whole-number field stores the magnitude on its own
options.misconception: believes a whole-number field keeps the fractional part somehow

questions.explanation: Truncating 4.6 keeps the 4 and throws the fraction away, while rounding keeps the 5, so the two differ by one whole step and only one of them matches the value that was measured. The tempting answer is B, which treats rounding as a warning rather than a different result, and it is wrong because the stored number itself changes. The tempting answer is C, which simply swaps the two, and a field that always moved up would overstate every reading it was given.
questions.hint: Write 4.6 down and ask what each method keeps as the final digit.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Checking a raw-code log against its range
questions.learningObjective: find the row of a sensor log that breaks its scaling rule
questions.stem: A 12-bit sensor spans 0 to 5 V across 4096 codes. Which row of this log is inconsistent with that rule?

options.text: raw 4096 recorded as 5.00 V, because 4096 is one code past the end of a 12-bit field
options.misconception: believes a 12-bit field reaches 4096 as a storable code

options.text: raw 2048 recorded as 2.50 V, because half the codes sit at half the range
options.misconception: believes half the codes of a range do not reach half the range

options.text: raw 3072 recorded as 3.75 V, because three quarters of the codes reach three quarters
options.misconception: believes three quarters of the codes fall short of three quarters

options.text: raw 1024 recorded as 1.25 V, because a quarter of the codes reach a quarter of the range
options.misconception: believes a quarter of the codes overshoot a quarter of the range

questions.explanation: A 12-bit field holds codes 0 to 4095, so 4096 was never a storable code and the row that records it as a reading cannot have come from this sensor. The other three rows are exactly the rule applied correctly, since 2048 of 4096 codes is half of 5 V and 3072 is three quarters of it, and their agreement is what makes the fourth row stand out. The tempting answer is any of those three consistent rows, and it fails because a row that obeys the rule cannot also be the one that breaks it, however plausible its decimals look.
questions.hint: Check the largest code the field can hold, then test each row against it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Reading signed patterns in a log
questions.learningObjective: find the row whose signed pattern contradicts its reading
questions.stem: Readings are stored in 4-bit two's complement fields. Which row of this log pairs a reading with a pattern that does not agree?

options.text: the row pairing 6 with 1110, because 1110 in four-bit two's complement is minus 2
options.misconception: believes the pattern 1110 stands for the positive value 6

options.text: the row pairing 3 with 0011, because a positive value needs its top bit set
options.misconception: believes only patterns with the top bit set can be positive

options.text: the row pairing -4 with 1100, because a negative value has to start with a zero
options.misconception: believes a negative reading must begin with a zero bit

options.text: the row pairing 7 with 0111, because 0111 is the largest pattern a field holds
options.misconception: believes the largest pattern stands for the largest value

questions.explanation: In four-bit two's complement the top bit carries the sign, so 1110 is minus 2 and the value 6 would be 0110, which makes that the one row where pattern and reading disagree. The tempting answer is B, which claims a positive value needs the top bit set, and that reverses the meaning of the top bit entirely. The tempting answer is also D, which is a true fact about 0111 and irrelevant, because 7 genuinely is that pattern and the row is correct.
questions.hint: Read each pattern as a signed 4-bit value and compare it with the reading.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: compute the size cost of a text-safe binary encoding
questions.stem: A transfer tool rewrites every 3 bytes of binary as 4 printable characters so the data can travel through a channel that only carries text. What does that rule cost?

options.text: One extra character per three bytes, so the text form is about a third larger
options.misconception: believes a text-safe encoding shrinks the data it protects

options.text: One extra byte per three characters, so the text form is about a third smaller
options.misconception: believes printable characters store fewer bytes than the raw bytes

options.text: Nothing at all, because a printable character still carries the same eight bits
options.misconception: believes printable and raw forms always occupy identical space

options.text: Two extra characters per three bytes, so the text form is about two thirds larger
options.misconception: believes three raw bytes need five printable characters

questions.explanation: Three bytes become four characters, which is one character of overhead for every three, so a 3000 byte file arrives as 4000 characters and the text form is a third larger. The tempting answer is B, which reverses the direction of the trade and would be the right answer if the tool were packing bytes into fewer characters, which is not what a text channel requires. The overhead is the price of making the data survive a channel that cannot carry the original bytes at all.
questions.hint: Work out how many characters 3000 bytes would become.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: count the unused codes left by a fixed-width alphabet
questions.stem: A code gives every letter of a 26 letter alphabet its own 6-bit field. How many of the 64 codes can that field hold, and what does the remainder cost?

options.text: 26 can be held, so 38 codes go unused and the width spends space on impossible letters
options.misconception: believes a 6-bit field must be filled completely by the alphabet

options.text: 64 can be held, so nothing goes unused and the width exactly fits the alphabet
options.misconception: believes 6 bits and 26 letters are an exact match

options.text: 38 can be held, so 26 codes go unused and the width is set by the data
options.misconception: believes the unused count is the number of codes the field can hold

options.text: 12 can be held, so 14 codes go unused and only vowels need codes here
options.misconception: believes an alphabet of 26 letters needs a separate code per vowel

questions.explanation: A 6-bit field offers 64 codes and the alphabet needs 26, so 38 codes are unreachable and the space they occupy is spent on letters that cannot occur in the text. The tempting answer is B, which reads the field's capacity as though it were the alphabet's requirement, and the two numbers are simply not the same thing. Fixed-width codes are chosen by rounding the alphabet up to the next power of two, and the leftover is the standing cost of that simplicity.
questions.hint: Subtract the number of letters from the number of codes the field offers.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Matching a scheme to a changing log
questions.learningObjective: choose delta coding for a slowly changing series
questions.stem: A weather station logs 4000 readings, one each minute, and each reading differs from the one before it by 0 or 1. Which scheme fits that pattern, and why?

options.text: Delta coding, because each record repeats the last value plus a change of almost nothing
options.misconception: believes a coding scheme should store whole readings rather than differences

options.text: Run-length coding, because readings that barely move form one long run of equal values
options.misconception: believes values that are close together count as equal for run coding

options.text: A fixed-width field per reading, because every reading needs the same 12 bits anyway
options.misconception: believes a fixed width is the cheapest option for any numeric log

options.text: A dictionary of whole readings, because each reading is a new value worth naming
options.misconception: believes a log of changing values is mostly made of repeats

questions.explanation: Delta coding stores the change from the previous reading, and a series that moves by 0 or 1 stores almost nothing at all, so it is the pattern the scheme is built for. The tempting answer is B, which treats nearly-equal as equal, and run-length coding needs genuinely equal values, since a 4000-value series that drifted by one each step has no runs to count. The tempting answer is also D, which assumes a repeating log, and drift means almost every reading appears exactly once.
questions.hint: Ask what most readings have in common, and what a code would have to store to capture that.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: choose dictionary coding for repeated multi-word phrases
questions.stem: A support log repeats the phrase password reset requested by 900 times inside 4000 records. Which scheme exploits that pattern best, and what does it charge for the table?

options.text: A dictionary of common phrases, since each later repeat costs a short reference instead of the words
options.misconception: believes repeated wording should still be stored in full every time

options.text: Run-length coding, since the phrase is one unbroken block of identical characters
options.misconception: believes a phrase is a run of equal characters that coding can count

options.text: A fixed-width field per phrase, since a fixed width removes repetition automatically
options.misconception: believes a fixed-width code cannot repeat the same value twice

options.text: Lossy compression, since wording that repeats carries no information worth keeping
options.misconception: believes repeated wording can be discarded without changing the record

questions.explanation: Dictionary coding names each common phrase once and then spends a short reference on every later appearance, so 900 occurrences of the same 31 characters stop costing 31 characters each. The tempting answer is B, which mistakes a phrase for a run; run-length coding counts equal consecutive characters, and the characters inside the phrase are all different. The tempting answer is also D, which would throw away the very text a support log exists to keep, and the cost of a dictionary is a one-off table rather than lost content.
questions.hint: Ask what the repeats have in common: whole phrases, or single equal characters.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: When a run coder makes a file longer
questions.learningObjective: predict the size effect of run coding on unpatterned data
questions.stem: A camera sensor log holds 400 bits in which no two adjacent bits are equal. A team runs run-length coding over it to save space. What happens to the file?

options.text: It gets longer, because every isolated bit needs its own run code in the output
options.misconception: believes a coding scheme can only ever make a file shorter

options.text: It stays the same length, because run-length coding never changes the stored size
options.misconception: believes a coder passes data through without adding information

options.text: It gets shorter, because coding always removes bits from the data it stores
options.misconception: believes compression removes bits rather than replacing them

options.text: It becomes half as long, because the runs account for half of all the bits
options.misconception: believes a data set with no repeats still has runs to count

questions.explanation: With no two adjacent bits equal there is one run per bit, so 400 bits need 400 run codes where each code carries a count and a value, and the output is larger than the input. The tempting answer is C, which treats compression as deletion, and it is wrong because a coder replaces runs with descriptions rather than deleting anything. The tempting answer is also B, which is true of a coder that chose not to encode at all, and that is the decision to make when runs are absent.
questions.hint: Count the runs first, then compare their number with the number of bits.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Packing flags instead of storing columns
questions.learningObjective: compute the space saved by packing flag columns
questions.stem: A 400 row attendance table has eight yes or no columns, and each column is currently stored as a full byte. What would packing the eight flags into one bit each save per row?

options.text: Seven bytes per row, because eight whole bytes collapse into a single byte
options.misconception: believes a yes or no value needs a whole byte of storage

options.text: Half a byte per row, because each flag occupies only half of its byte
options.misconception: believes packing reduces each flag to half of its original size

options.text: Nothing per row, because a byte is the smallest unit a table can store
options.misconception: believes storage units set a floor that packing cannot cross

options.text: Six bytes per row, because only seven of the eight flags are worth keeping
options.misconception: believes one of the eight flags needs no storage at all

questions.explanation: Eight flags at one bit each use exactly one byte, so a row that cost eight bytes now costs one and the saving is seven bytes per row, which is 2800 bytes across 400 rows. The tempting answer is B, which halves each flag rather than shrinking it to a bit, and a yes or no value has no fractional part to preserve. The tempting answer is also C, which mistakes a storage unit for a minimum payload; a byte is a unit of transfer, not a floor on what a value occupies.
questions.hint: Multiply eight flags by one bit and convert the result to bytes.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: choose a scheme that fits a limit without losing readings
questions.stem: A club must keep all 2000 daily readings in under 4 KB. Three measured options: run-length coding gives 5.6 KB, dictionary coding gives 3.1 KB, and halving the sample rate gives 1.2 KB. Which option is right, and what decides it?

options.text: Dictionary coding, because it clears the limit while keeping every one of the 2000 readings
options.misconception: believes the smallest result is always the right result to keep

options.text: Halving the sample rate, because it is the only option that clearly fits the limit
options.misconception: believes fitting the limit is the whole of the requirement

options.text: Run-length coding, because compressing a numeric log is the conventional first choice
options.misconception: believes a numeric log must be compressed with a coder built for repeats

options.text: Either of the two that fit, since the size limit is the only requirement stated
options.misconception: believes the requirement to keep every reading is already satisfied

questions.explanation: Two requirements apply at once, the file must stay under 4 KB and all 2000 readings must survive, and only dictionary coding meets both, at 3.1 KB with nothing discarded. The tempting answer is B, which optimises the size constraint alone; halving the sample rate is smaller but silently deletes half the readings, which is a smaller file of a different and less useful data set. The tempting answer is C, which picks a coder by habit, and run-length coding actually exceeds the limit here because drifting readings contain no runs to count.
questions.hint: Check the limit and the data requirement separately for each option.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Questions a scheme choice must answer
questions.learningObjective: identify the requirements that decide a compression choice
questions.stem: A team must pick a compression scheme for a log they still have to be able to read back. Which TWO questions must be settled before any scheme is chosen? Select exactly two.

options.text: Can the data be reconstructed exactly, or will the scheme discard readings
Is the scheme the one most teams use, so the file will be easy to share
options.misconception: believes popularity decides whether a file stays readable

options.text: Does the pattern in the data match what the scheme is good at shrinking
Will the compressed file open in a text editor, so it can be inspected by eye
options.misconception: believes a compressed file should be readable without decoding it

questions.explanation: A scheme can only be judged against two things, whether the data comes back exactly and whether the pattern in it is the pattern the scheme exploits, so those two answers eliminate most candidates immediately. The tempting answer is B, which is a real consideration for sharing but says nothing about whether the scheme fits the data or preserves it. The tempting answer is also D, which asks a compressed file to be readable without being decoded, which rules out every scheme worth having.
questions.hint: Ask which questions narrow the list of schemes and which are just preferences.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Reading a compression ratio as a saving
questions.learningObjective: convert a before and after size into a percentage saved
questions.stem: A sensor log file of 48 KB is compressed to 12 KB. What percentage of the original file size was saved?
questions.explanation: The saving is 48 - 12 = 36 KB out of the original 48 KB, and 36 divided by 48 is 0.75, so three quarters of the size was removed. The common mistake is to divide by the smaller figure, which would report a ratio of 4 to 1 and is a different statement about the same two numbers, so the base of the percentage has to be the original size. A quarter of the original, the new file, is what remains on disk.
questions.hint: Subtract the new size from the old, then divide by the old size.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: infer frequency from the code lengths a compressor assigns
questions.stem: A compressor assigns these code lengths: 1 bit to A, 1 bit to B, 2 bits to C, 3 bits to D, and 4 bits to E. Which letter appeared most often in the data it compressed?

options.text: A, because a short code only pays off when the symbol is a common one
options.misconception: believes a short code can be given to a rare symbol without loss

options.text: E, because the longest code is reserved for the most frequent symbol
options.misconception: believes the longest code marks the commonest symbol

options.text: C, because a middle length balances a symbol's rank with its frequency
options.misconception: believes a middle code length always marks the commonest symbol

options.text: D, because a three-bit code is the average of the lengths assigned
options.misconception: believes an average code length marks the most frequent symbol

questions.explanation: The point of variable-length coding is that a frequent symbol is cheap to write, so the one-bit codes belong to the two commonest letters and A is among them. The tempting answer is B, which reverses the economics, because a long code is the sensible choice for a rare symbol and would be wasteful for a common one. The tempting answer is also D, which reads a table of numbers and finds the middle, and the average of these lengths says nothing about any single symbol's frequency.
questions.hint: Ask which assignment makes the compressed file smallest for a given text.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Choosing a scheme for a stated pattern
questions.learningObjective: justify a compression choice against a stated pattern and constraint
questions.stem: A 5000 line factory log uses 60 distinct status words that appear in long runs, and every line must be recoverable exactly. Which scheme fits, and what decides it?

options.text: A dictionary of the 60 status words, because long runs make short references pay off
options.misconception: believes repeated whole words gain nothing from being named once

options.text: A lossy shrink, because the words repeat often enough that detail can be dropped
options.misconception: believes repetition makes a line safe to discard parts of

options.text: A fixed-width code per word, because a fixed width keeps every record the same size
options.misconception: believes uniform record sizes are what the requirement asks for

options.text: Run-length coding per character, because character runs beat whole-word references
options.misconception: believes character-level runs are always better than word references

questions.explanation: Naming each of the 60 words once costs a small table, and the long runs then cost a reference per word, so the saving scales with how much the log repeats; exact recovery is preserved because the table and the references rebuild the original lines. The tempting answer is B, which mistakes repetition for dispensability, and a log that has to be recovered exactly cannot afford a scheme that decides some of it does not matter. The tempting answer is D, which mixes two levels, since coding characters inside a word is wasted work when the whole word is already known.
questions.hint: Ask what repeats in this log, and whether anything may be discarded.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a decimal to binary conversion
questions.stem: Put these steps in the order they must happen to convert the decimal number 50 into binary by hand.

options.text: Divide 50 by 2, write down the remainder, and keep the quotient for the next pass
options.misconception: writing the last quotient instead of its remainder drops the leading bit

options.text: Read the collected remainders from the last pass back to the first to form the bit string
options.misconception: reading the remainders in the order collected reverses the digits

options.text: Stop once the quotient reaches 0, since a zero quotient ends the conversion
options.misconception: stopping while the quotient is still 1 drops the leading bit of the answer

options.text: Convert the finished bit string back to decimal as a check on the work
options.misconception: skipping the check leaves a mistaken digit-order reading undetected

questions.explanation: Each pass produces one remainder and the collection grows from the least significant bit, so the digits are only correct once they are read back, and the final zero quotient marks the end of the work. For 50 the collected remainders are 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1 and reading them backwards gives 110010, which is 32 + 16 + 2. The tempting inversion puts B first and reads them as collected, which yields 19 because the digits are correct but reversed, and the other inversion stops at C one pass early, dropping the leading 1 and giving 18.
questions.hint: Collect first, read back second, and check the result at the end.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a code cannot grow within its width
questions.learningObjective: explain a fixed ceiling on the number of characters a width supports
questions.stem: A badge system's code gives 7 bits per character, so it can name 128 characters, and the team now needs 200 distinct names. Explain in a short paragraph why the same 7 bits cannot be stretched to cover them.

answer.exemplar: Seven bits provide 2 to the power 7, which is 128, distinct bit patterns, and each pattern can stand for exactly one character, so 128 is a hard ceiling rather than a starting point. Two hundred names need 2 to the power 8, which is 256 patterns, so the field must widen to 8 bits; reassigning, reordering, or sharing the existing codes cannot manufacture patterns the width does not contain. The limit is set by the width before any code is chosen, which is why no cleverer table fixes it. Widening to 8 bits also costs 4 bits more per character, so the fix is not free.

questions.explanation: A complete answer states that 7 bits give exactly 128 patterns, that a pattern names one character, and that 200 names therefore require 8 bits; it also notes that no rearrangement of the existing codes can create patterns. An answer that only says the table needs to be bigger misses the reason, since a table is a list of codes drawn from the field's patterns. The strongest answers add the storage cost, because widening a field is a real expense rather than a free correction.
questions.hint: Ask how many distinct patterns a 7-bit field can hold at all.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain why more bits do not fix a sampling problem
questions.stem: A field team doubles the bit depth of its sound recorder from 8 to 16 bits per sample, keeps the sample rate at 8000 samples per second, and still cannot hear a 5000 Hz tone correctly. Explain in a short paragraph why the extra bits did not help.

answer.exemplar: Bit depth sets how finely each sample's amplitude is recorded, while the sample rate sets how much of the frequency range is captured at all. A 5000 Hz tone sampled 8000 times a second is sampled fewer than twice per cycle, so the samples do not describe the waveform and the tone is reconstructed wrongly no matter how precisely each sample was measured. The team was fighting a sampling error, not a quantisation error, and 16 bits reduces the second kind only. The setting to change is the sample rate, which has to be high enough that the highest frequency of interest is sampled many times per cycle.

questions.explanation: A complete answer separates the two settings, names the fault as sampling rather than quantisation, and says the sample rate is what must change; an answer that only says more bits is better is missing the distinction entirely. The strongest answers add that each setting is chosen against a different limit, the sample rate against the highest frequency of interest and the depth against the smallest amplitude worth recording. Naming the aliasing effect by name is a bonus rather than the requirement.
questions.hint: Ask what each setting controls, then count samples per cycle of the tone.
